column3: An amide's C-N unit is nearly planar and has a larger rotational barrier than the C-N bond of an ordinary amine. A resonance contributor places a C=N bond, positive charge on N and negative charge on O. Which interpretation connects these observations?
column4: The amide rapidly alternates between two separately isolable charged molecules
column5: The amide nitrogen must have five covalent bonds in its ground state
column6: Electron delocalisation gives partial C-N double-bond character, so twisting weakens conjugation
column7: The C-N barrier proves the carbonyl oxygen is not bonded to carbon
column9:
Answer: (C) Delocalisation gives partial C-N double-bond character.
Why: Donation of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl system links the nitrogen and carbonyl orbitals. A planar arrangement supports overlap and gives the actual C-N bond more multiple-bond character than an isolated amine C-N bond. Twisting reduces that overlap, costing energy. The charged drawing is a contributor to one delocalised electronic structure, not evidence that the molecule spends alternating intervals in separately isolable forms.
Why not the others: (A) replaces a resonance hybrid by a kinetic equilibrium of drawings. (B) violates the ordinary nitrogen valence count; the contributor has an octet, not five bonds. (D) contradicts the carbonyl connectivity retained in both contributors.
Key point: Use resonance to explain measurable bond properties without treating contributors as separate molecules.

column3: The schematic represents \(\ce{[Co2(en)4(OH)2]^4+}\). Each en chelates one cobalt through two N atoms; each of the two OH groups bridges both cobalt centres through its O atom. All other donor connections are shown. What are the oxidation state and coordination number of each equivalent cobalt?
column9:
Answer: (A) +3 and coordination number 6.
Given: Four neutral en ligands, two hydroxide ions and overall charge +4; the two metals are equivalent.
Formula/Principle: Charge balance determines oxidation state; count donor atoms attached to each metal for coordination number.
Step 1: \[2x+4(0)+2(-1)=+4\ \Rightarrow\ x=+3.\]
Step 2: Each cobalt receives four N donors from its two en ligands and two O donors from the bridges: \[\mathrm{CN}=4+2=6.\]
Why: A bridging oxygen counts as one donor to each metal it actually contacts. Ligand count for the entire ion is therefore not the coordination number of either cobalt. Likewise a neutral chelator contributes donor atoms without contributing ionic charge.
Why not the others: (B) neglects the hydroxide charges in oxidation-state balance. (C) counts only chelate donors and omits the bridges. (D) counts the whole ion's chelate donors at one metal and assigns the wrong charge.
Key point: Count charge globally but donor contacts locally in a multinuclear complex.

column3: The figure gives two allowed carbon-atom configurations: P is 1s2 2s2 2p2 with the p electrons unpaired in different orbitals; Q is 1s2 2s1 2p3 with parallel p spins. Ignoring orbital contributions to magnetism, which comparison is correct?
column4: Q is forbidden because a 2s electron cannot be promoted
column5: P and Q have equal energy because electron number is equal
column6: P has four unpaired electrons and Q has two
column7: P has two unpaired electrons; Q has four and is excited relative to P
column9:
Answer: (D) P has two unpaired electrons, Q four, and Q is excited.
Why: P has a paired 2s orbital and two singly occupied p orbitals, giving two unpaired electrons. Q has a singly occupied 2s and three singly occupied p orbitals, giving four. Both preserve six electrons and obey Pauli exclusion, but Q promotes an electron from lower-energy 2s to 2p in this multielectron atom. The promotion costs energy even though it increases the number of unpaired electrons.
Why not the others: (A) confuses an excited state with an exclusion-rule violation. (B) assumes electron count alone fixes electronic energy. (C) reverses the occupations shown.
Key point: Check allowed occupancy separately from whether a configuration is the lowest-energy one.

column3: In acid-catalysed addition to a carbonyl compound, the carbonyl oxygen first uses a lone pair to bind H+. Which description of that first step and its consequence is correct?
column4: Carbonyl carbon donates a pair to H+, making it less electrophilic
column5: Oxygen acts as a nucleophile towards H+, and protonation increases carbonyl-carbon electrophilicity
column6: H+ donates an electron pair to oxygen and becomes a radical
column7: Protonation removes the carbonyl carbon from the molecule
column9:
Answer: (B) Oxygen donates to H+ and activates the carbonyl carbon.
Why: A nucleophile supplies the electron pair used to form a new bond. Here the carbonyl oxygen is the donor and the proton is the electron-pair acceptor. Protonation increases the electron deficiency of the conjugated carbonyl system, making carbon more susceptible to a subsequent nucleophilic attack. Roles are assigned for the specific step; an atom's role in one event does not require it to be the attack site in the next.
Why not the others: (A) assigns pair donation to the wrong atom and reverses the activation effect. (C) gives a proton an electron pair it does not possess and introduces radical chemistry. (D) changes the carbon skeleton without any carbon-cleavage step.
Key point: Follow electron-pair origin and destination rather than assigning nucleophile and electrophile labels by charge alone.

column3: Toluene is chlorinated in separate trials. X uses light and conditions favouring one side-chain substitution. Y uses Cl2/FeCl3 in the dark under ring-substitution conditions. Which products best distinguish the two pathways?
column4: X mainly o/p-chlorotoluene; Y benzyl chloride
column5: Both mainly benzyl chloride because methyl always reacts first
column6: X mainly benzyl chloride; Y mainly o/p-chlorotoluene
column7: Both mainly m-chlorotoluene because chlorine is deactivating
column9:
Answer: (C) X gives benzyl chloride and Y ring-chlorinated ortho/para products.
Why: Light promotes radical halogenation at the benzylic side chain, where radical stabilisation supports replacement of a methyl hydrogen. Lewis-acid-assisted chlorination instead supplies an electrophile for aromatic substitution. The pre-existing methyl group directs that ring substitution mainly to ortho and para positions. The directing group relevant to the first ring substitution is methyl, not a chlorine atom that has not yet been attached.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the stated radical and electrophilic conditions. (B) ignores the change in reaction mechanism caused by illumination and catalyst. (D) uses the wrong directing group and wrongly makes its deactivation imply meta direction.

column3: A student proposes preparing pure propane by the Wurtz reaction of an equimolar mixture of methyl bromide and ethyl bromide with sodium in dry ether. Assuming both self-coupling and cross-coupling occur, why is the proposal unsuitable for a single pure product?
column4: Ethane, propane and butane can all form
column5: Only methane can form because sodium removes carbon
column6: Propane cannot form because unlike alkyl groups never couple
column7: All coupling products must have an odd number of carbons
column9:
Answer: (A) Ethane, propane and butane can form.
Why: Joining two methyl groups gives ethane, joining methyl with ethyl gives propane, and joining two ethyl groups gives butane. A mixed-halide Wurtz reaction therefore does not uniquely specify the desired cross-coupling product. The argument concerns competing carbon-group pairings, not an inability to make any propane. It also explains why symmetric alkane preparation is more straightforward with a single suitable halide.
Why not the others: (B) invents carbon removal instead of coupling. (C) excludes the cross-pairing that is explicitly allowed. (D) ignores the even-carbon products of both self-pairings.
Key point: List all allowed coupling partners before treating a mixed-halide reaction as a selective synthesis.

column3: The structure is \(\ce{C6H5-O-CH2-CH2-O-CH3}\). It is heated with excess HI until ether cleavage and conversion of the resulting ordinary aliphatic alcohol groups to iodides are complete. Assume substitution without elimination or skeletal rearrangement; the aryl-O bond is retained. Which final organic product set and minimum HI consumption per mole of starting ether are correct?
column4: Iodobenzene, ethane-1,2-diol and methane; 2 mol HI
column5: Phenol, 2-iodoethanol and methyl iodide; 2 mol HI
column6: Phenol, ethane and methyl iodide; 3 mol HI
column7: Phenol, 1,2-diiodoethane and methyl iodide; 3 mol HI
column9:
Answer: (D) Phenol, 1,2-diiodoethane and methyl iodide; 3 mol HI.
Given: Both ether links are cleaved, ordinary aliphatic OH is converted further, and aryl-O cleavage is excluded.
Formula/Principle: HI cleaves alkyl-O bonds; a generated aliphatic alcohol can consume another HI to form an iodide.
Step 1: Cleaving the phenoxyethyl bond can give \[\ce{Ph-O-CH2-CH2-O-CH3 + HI -> PhOH + I-CH2-CH2-O-CH3}.\]
Step 2: Attack at the methyl end gives \[\ce{I-CH2-CH2-O-CH3 + HI -> I-CH2-CH2-OH + CH3I}.\]
Step 3: Continued reaction converts the remaining alcohol: \[\ce{I-CH2-CH2-OH + HI -> I-CH2-CH2-I + H2O}.\]
Step 4: Summing consumes three HI and conserves all nine carbons among phenol, the two-carbon diiodide and methyl iodide. A different order of ether cleavages gives the same final set under the stated completion conditions.
Why: The resistant aryl-O bond leaves phenol as the aryl-containing product. Stopping after the two original ether cleavages would overlook the reactive aliphatic OH formed along the route. The explicit assumptions exclude competing elimination so that functional-group and atom accounting identify a single final set.
Why not the others: (A) breaks the excluded aryl-O bond and invents reduction to methane. (B) stops at a reactive alcohol before the stated completion. (C) replaces two C-I substitutions by reduction to ethane.
Key point: Under excess-reagent conditions, continue through reactive intermediates before counting final products and equivalents.

column3: An ester has formula C4H8O2. Complete hydrolysis produces a carboxylic acid and an alcohol, which are separated. The alcohol gives a positive iodoform test under standard conditions. Which ester is consistent?
column9:
Answer: (C) Ethyl ethanoate.
Why: Among the proposed C4 esters, ethyl ethanoate releases ethanol, which is oxidised under iodoform conditions to the required methyl-carbonyl system. Methyl propanoate releases methanol, and propyl methanoate releases propan-1-ol, neither of which gives that standard positive test. Separation matters because the test is being assigned specifically to the alcohol fragment rather than to the original mixture. The molecular formula independently excludes the C3 ester.
Why not the others: (A) gives methanol rather than ethanol. (B) gives propan-1-ol, which lacks the required alcohol arrangement for a positive test. (D) has formula C3H6O2 and also gives methanol.
Key point: Use hydrolysis to map an ester's two carbon fragments before applying a diagnostic product test.

column3: Which sequence converts aniline to benzoic acid while increasing the organic carbon count by one, without retaining nitrogen in the final product?
column4: Diazotisation at 0-5 C, CuCN substitution, then nitrile hydrolysis
column5: Diazotisation, replacement by H, then amide hydrolysis
column6: Acetylation followed by Hofmann degradation of the ring
column7: Bromination followed only by reduction of the C-Br bond
column9:
Answer: (A) Diazotisation, cyanide substitution and nitrile hydrolysis.
Why: Diazotisation converts the amino group into a leaving diazonium group. Copper-cyanide substitution introduces a carbon-containing CN group directly on the ring, giving benzonitrile and adding one carbon to the original six. Hydrolysis converts the nitrile carbon into a carboxyl carbon and removes its nitrogen into an inorganic nitrogen-containing product. The carbon count therefore increases while the final benzoic acid contains no nitrogen.
Why not the others: (B) removes the amino substituent without introducing the extra carbon. (C) misapplies Hofmann degradation and does not place a carboxyl group on the ring. (D) only changes a halogen substituent and supplies no new carbon.
Key point: Cyanide substitution followed by hydrolysis is a carbon-adding route to an aromatic carboxylic acid.

column3: A dilute ideal electrolyte has measured van't Hoff factor i=5. Assume complete dissociation into simple ions, with no association or reaction. Its ions and charges are otherwise unknown. Which conclusion is justified from this measurement alone?
column4: The formula must be A2B3 and no other stoichiometry is possible
column5: Five ionic particles form per formula unit, but the formula is not uniquely determined
column6: Each ion must carry charge magnitude five
column7: The formula must contain exactly five different elements
column9:
Answer: (B) Five ions form per formula unit, without unique formula determination.
Why: Under the specified complete-dissociation model, i is the ratio of solute-particle amount to analytical formula-unit amount. It therefore counts the total number of separated ions produced. Several charge-balanced stoichiometries can supply five ions, such as A2B3 with suitable 3+/2- charges or AB4 with suitable 4+/1- charges. A colligative measurement by itself does not identify ionic charges or chemical elements.
Why not the others: (A) claims uniqueness without charge or composition evidence. (C) confuses particle number with charge magnitude. (D) equates the number of particles with the number of distinct elements.
Key point: A colligative particle count can constrain stoichiometry without uniquely identifying a salt.

column3: A conductivity cell gives resistance 100 ohm for a reference solution with conductivity 0.0140 S/cm. In the same cell, a monoprotic weak acid of concentration 0.0100 mol/L has resistance 1400 ohm. Its limiting molar conductivity is 400 S cm2/mol. Using an ideal dissociation model, what is Ka?
column9:
Answer: (C) \(8.33	imes10^{-4}\) M.
Given: Reference conductivity and resistance calibrate one fixed cell; acid concentration and limiting molar conductivity are supplied.
Formula/Principle: Cell constant \(g=\kappa R\), \(\Lambda_m=1000\kappa/c\), \(\alpha=\Lambda_m/\Lambda_m^\infty\), and \(K_a=c\alpha^2/(1-\alpha)\).
Step 1: \[g=0.0140(100)=1.40	ext{ cm}^{-1},\quad \kappa_{HA}=1.40/1400=0.00100	ext{ S/cm}.\]
Step 2: \[\Lambda_m=1000(0.00100)/0.0100=100	ext{ S cm}^2/	ext{mol},\quad\alpha=100/400=0.250.\]
Step 3: \[K_a= rac{0.0100(0.250)^2}{0.750}=8.33	imes10^{-4}	ext{ M}.\]
Why: Resistance depends on cell geometry, so the reference must first establish the cell constant. The molar conductivity ratio estimates the ionised fraction under the ideal model. A 25% dissociation is too large to silently replace 1-alpha by one, so the full denominator is retained.
Why not the others: (A) uses c times alpha rather than the equilibrium concentration ratio. (B) omits the undissociated-acid denominator. (D) assumes complete acid dissociation from the existence of a conductive solution.
Key point: Calibrate conductance geometry before extracting dissociation and retain a non-negligible ionisation correction.

column3: Two independent first-order reactions X and Y have temperature-independent Arrhenius parameters. At 300 K, kX/kY=4; at 600 K, kX/kY=1. At 400 K, their initial reactant concentrations obey [X]0/[Y]0=3. What is the ratio of their initial disappearance rates at 400 K?
column9:
Answer: (B) 6.
Given: Both reactions are first order; two rate-constant ratios constrain their Arrhenius difference.
Formula/Principle: \(\ln(k_X/k_Y)=\ln(A_X/A_Y)-(E_X-E_Y)/(RT)\) is linear in 1/T, not T.
Step 1: The reciprocal temperature at 400 K is the midpoint: \[ rac1{400}= rac12\left( rac1{300}+ rac1{600}ight).\]
Step 2: Consequently \[\ln(k_X/k_Y)_{400}=	frac12(\ln4+\ln1)=\ln2,\] so the rate-constant ratio is 2.
Step 3: Initial rates include concentration: \[ rac{v_X}{v_Y}= rac{k_X[X]_0}{k_Y[Y]_0}=2(3)=6.\]
Step 4: As a consistency check, the ratio declines on warming, so the X reaction has the smaller activation energy under these assumptions.
Why: Comparing two Arrhenius equations eliminates the need to know either absolute rate constant. Interpolation must use inverse temperature because that is the linear variable. A rate-constant ratio becomes a reaction-rate ratio only after including the concentration factors and the stated first-order law.
Why not the others: (A) ignores the rate-constant difference. (C) reports the rate-constant ratio alone. (D) uses the 300 K ratio at 400 K.
Key point: Interpolate Arrhenius ratios in reciprocal temperature, then distinguish rate constants from rates.

column3: At a fixed temperature, K1=4 for \(\ce{A <=> B}\) and K2=8 for \(\ce{A <=> C}\), using dimensionless activities. What are K and the sign of the standard Gibbs change for \(\ce{2B <=> A + C}\)?
column9:
Answer: (D) K=1/2 and the standard Gibbs change is positive.
Given: Two equilibria share A at one temperature.
Formula/Principle: Reaction addition multiplies constants; reversal inverts K and doubling squares it.
Step 1: Reverse and double the first reaction: \[\ce{2B <=> 2A},\quad K'=1/4^2=1/16.\]
Step 2: Add \(\ce{A <=> C}\), cancelling one A: \[K=(1/16)(8)=1/2.\]
Step 3: \[\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K=RT\ln2>0.\]
Why: Equilibrium constants belong to specified stoichiometric equations. Changing coefficients changes the exponent pattern in the activity quotient. The standard Gibbs sign is then determined by whether the resulting dimensionless K lies above or below one; it does not specify the actual direction for every nonstandard composition.
Why not the others: (A) divides by K1 only once instead of squaring it. (B) multiplies the original constants without reversing or doubling. (C) reverses the sign in the Gibbs-constant relation.
Key point: Manipulate the reaction equation before manipulating its equilibrium constant.

column3: At 25 C, a monoprotic acid has analytical concentration 10^-8 M and Ka=10^-5. Water has Kw=10^-14. With no other solutes, which pH description is correct?
column4: Slightly below 7, with water autoionisation important
column5: Exactly 8 because -log of the acid concentration is 8
column7: Exactly 5 because pH always equals pKa
column9:
Answer: (A) Slightly below 7.
Why: The acid concentration is smaller than the hydrogen-ion concentration of pure water. Charge balance requires hydrogen ions to balance both hydroxide and the acid anion, so acid addition cannot make this solution alkaline. Most of this very dilute acid is ionised because Ka greatly exceeds the resulting hydrogen-ion concentration, but water remains a major source of both ions. Neglecting water or assuming a small ionised fraction is therefore inconsistent.
Given: \(C=10^{-8}\) M, \(K_a=10^{-5}\), \(K_w=10^{-14}\).
Formula/Principle: Charge balance is \([H^+]=[OH^-]+[A^-]\), with \(0<[A^-]<C\).
Step 1: The bounds imply \[10^{-7}<[H^+]< rac{C+\sqrt{C^2+4K_w}}2\approx1.052	imes10^{-7}	ext{ M}.\]
Step 2: Hence \(6.978<\mathrm{pH}<7\), confirming a small acidic shift.
Why not the others: (B) ignores water and even predicts alkalinity from an acid. (C) uses the small-dissociation approximation where its predicted dissociation exceeds the total acid. (D) assumes a buffer equality that is not present.
Key point: Very dilute acid solutions require water and charge balance even when the acid is weak.

column3: Zr and Hf commonly form +4 compounds with very similar ionic sizes, although Hf has a much larger atomic mass. Which explanation and inference are most appropriate?
column4: Mass alone forces Hf compounds to have a different valence from Zr compounds
column5: The two elements must have identical densities, isotope masses and all spectra
column6: The similarity proves Hf has no f electrons in any preceding element
column7: The intervening lanthanoid contraction helps give similar sizes and chemistry; equal mass-related properties do not follow
column9:
Answer: (D) Lanthanoid contraction helps explain similar size and chemistry.
Why: Poor shielding by added 4f electrons across the intervening lanthanoid series increases effective nuclear attraction and contracts later atomic and ionic sizes. Hf therefore resembles Zr in size and in many +4 chemical behaviours more closely than a simple extra-shell expectation would suggest. Atomic mass is a separate property and can differ greatly even when ionic radius and common oxidation state are similar.
Why not the others: (A) treats mass as a direct valence rule. (C) contradicts the role of the intervening filled 4f series and confuses Hf chemistry with a claim about preceding atoms. (B) generalises a size/chemistry similarity to every mass-dependent or spectroscopic property.
Key point: A periodic size explanation supports related chemistry without making two elements physically identical.
